fields.definition: The high, thin, nasal sustained tone characteristic of the rebab, a bowed spike fiddle of the Middle East, North Africa, and Southeast Asia; the sound arises from a small resonating body and bowed strings rich in upper harmonics, giving a penetrating, reedy voice often likened to a whine.
fields.plain_english: A whine is the thin, high, nose-like sound of the rebab, a small bowed fiddle. Because its body is tiny and the bow keeps the string going, the tone stays bright and cuts right through the music.
fields.purpose_function: Names the rebab's signature timbre so engineers and players can recognize, capture, and control the instrument's bright, penetrating character within a mix.
fields.practical_application: A technician close-mics the rebab and may tame harsh upper mids with EQ so the whine stays present and expressive without becoming piercing in a folk or world-music recording.
common_mistakes: Cranking high-frequency EQ to add brightness, which makes the whine harsh and fatiguing
Confusing the rebab's natural nasal tone with a fault in the mic or signal chain
Gating too aggressively and cutting the sustained bowed tail
scenario_contexts: Miking a rebab for a world-music or film-score session
Blending a rebab against a string section in a fusion arrangement
Taming harsh upper mids on a solo rebab line during mixing

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Rabab/Rebab"
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (bowed-string acoustics and radiation)

fields.definition: The bright, metallic, sustaining resonance produced by the spun-metal cone of a resonator (Dobro-style) guitar; driven by the bridge like a mechanical loudspeaker, the cone radiates the string energy with a characteristic ringing, bell-like sustain and strong upper-mid content.
fields.plain_english: The ring is the bright, bell-like sustain that comes from the metal cone inside a resonator guitar. The cone works like a small speaker, so the notes ring out longer and sound more metallic than on a normal acoustic.
fields.purpose_function: Describes the core tonal signature of resonator guitars so engineers can capture and preserve the ringing, sustaining character that defines blues, bluegrass, and country resonator tones.
fields.practical_application: A technician positions a mic between the cone and the body ports, a few feet back, to capture the ring and body warmth without exaggerating pick and slide noise.
common_mistakes: Miking directly on the cone, which captures pick noise instead of the full ring
Over-compressing and squashing the natural ringing sustain
Assuming all resonators sound alike regardless of single-cone (biscuit or spider) or tricone design
scenario_contexts: Recording a Dobro for a bluegrass or country track
Capturing bottleneck slide blues on a single-cone resonator
Balancing resonator ring against a vocal in a mix

sources: Sound on Sound, "Recording Resonator Guitars" (Michael Messer, resonator technical technique feature)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (plate/cone radiation and driven-resonator behavior)

fields.definition: Acoustic feedback that occurs when an amplified resonator guitar's cone, designed to pick up and radiate string energy, is re-excited by sound arriving from monitors or the PA, producing a sustained howl or ring at the loop's resonant frequency.
fields.plain_english: Feedback is the loud howl that starts when a resonator guitar's cone picks up sound from the speakers and feeds it back around in a loop. Because the cone is built to grab and boost vibration, it feeds back more easily than a solid guitar.
fields.purpose_function: Warns that the resonator's amplifying cone makes it especially prone to feedback on stage, so technicians plan gain structure, monitor levels, and EQ to keep it under control.
fields.practical_application: A technician lowers monitor level, notches the ringing frequency with EQ, or blocks the body ports to stop a resonator from howling during a loud live set.
common_mistakes: UNSAFE: Pushing overall system or monitor gain to hear the resonator, which can trigger a sudden loud feedback howl that risks hearing damage and blown drivers
Blaming the PA rather than the resonator's cone for stage feedback
Notching so many frequencies that the guitar tone is hollowed out
scenario_contexts: A resonator player steps toward a monitor and the instrument begins to howl
Setting gain structure for an amplified resonator at soundcheck
Ringing out monitors to raise the feedback threshold for a resonator player

sources: Sound on Sound, "Recording Resonator Guitars" (resonator cone amplifies and feeds back through monitors)
Yamaha Sound Reinforcement Handbook (Davis & Jones, acoustic feedback and gain before feedback)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (feedback and system gain structure)

fields.definition: An unwanted buzzing or rattling noise from a resonator guitar caused by a loose or improperly seated cone, spider, coverplate, tailpiece, or hardware vibrating against the body or against itself when the strings are played.
fields.plain_english: A rattle is a buzzing noise from a resonator guitar. It happens when a loose part, like the metal cone or cover plate, shakes against the body. It usually means a part needs tightening, not that the guitar is broken.
fields.purpose_function: Flags a mechanical noise fault so a technician can locate and fix the loose component before it spoils a recording or performance.
fields.practical_application: A technician isolates the buzz by muting strings and tapping parts, then reseats the cone or snugs the coverplate hardware to silence the rattle.
common_mistakes: Assuming the rattle is a bad string or amp fault when it is actually loose resonator hardware
Overtightening coverplate screws and distorting the cone seat
Ignoring a faint rattle that a close mic will clearly capture on a quiet recording
scenario_contexts: Tracking a Dobro and hearing a buzz on certain notes
Pre-gig inspection of a resonator for loose hardware
Diagnosing a rattle that only appears at high playing volume

sources: Sound on Sound, "Recording Resonator Guitars" (mechanical/hardware noise in resonator capture)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (coupled-part vibration and buzzing in string instruments)

fields.definition: A rapid, even alternation of down-and-up plectrum (risha) strokes on the oud or buzuq that sustains a pitch or fills a phrase, producing the continuous, shimmering tremolo texture common in Arabic and Turkish string music.
fields.plain_english: Risha tremolo is fast back-and-forth picking on an oud, using the thin pick called a risha. The quick strokes blur into one long, shimmering note, the way a mandolin player holds a note.
fields.purpose_function: Names the technique that lets a plucked oud sustain a tone or ornament a melody, since a single pluck decays quickly.
fields.practical_application: An engineer captures the fine stroke detail of risha tremolo with a close condenser mic and avoids heavy transient limiting that would flatten the shimmer.
common_mistakes: Confusing tremolo (fast repeated notes) with vibrato (a pitch wobble)
Heavy transient shaping that smears the individual strokes into mush
Miking too far away and losing the crisp stroke detail
scenario_contexts: Recording an oud taqsim that uses tremolo on sustained notes
Blending an oud tremolo bed under a vocal line
Editing a tremolo passage where stroke evenness matters

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Oud" and "Tremolo" (plectrum tremolo articulation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (transient/sustain envelope and capture)

fields.definition: The sharp initial transient produced when a plectrum strikes the string on plucked lutes of the Middle East and South Asia — the risha (oud, buzuq) or the wire mizrab worn on the finger (sitar, sarod) — giving each note its percussive onset and defining the music's rhythmic articulation.
fields.plain_english: The attack is the sharp pluck sound at the very start of a note when a pick hits the string. On an oud the pick is a risha; on a sitar or sarod it is a metal finger pick called a mizrab. This crisp start gives the music its rhythmic bite.
fields.purpose_function: Describes the onset transient that carries the rhythm and clarity of plucked-lute lines, which engineers must preserve for definition in a mix.
fields.practical_application: A technician sets preamp and converter headroom so the sharp mizrab or risha attack is not clipped, and uses gentle compression to even out onsets without dulling them.
common_mistakes: Using fast, hard compression that dulls the plectrum attack
Setting record levels too hot and clipping the sharp transient
Confusing the metal mizrab's bright attack with digital distortion
scenario_contexts: Recording a sitar where each mizrab stroke must stay crisp
Tracking an oud rhythm part that drives the groove
Setting gain staging to protect sharp plucked transients from clipping

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Mizrab," "Sitar," and "Oud" (plectrum types and stroke articulation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (attack transients, envelope, and headroom)

fields.definition: The bright, sustained, glistening decay of the santoor (santur), a hammered dulcimer whose many courses of metal strings, struck with light mallets, ring and reinforce one another to create a shimmering wash of overtones.
fields.plain_english: Shimmer is the bright, sparkling sound that lingers after a santoor is struck. It has many metal strings hit with small hammers, and they all ring together, like sunlight on water, leaving a glowing tail.
fields.purpose_function: Names the santoor's signature sustained, overtone-rich decay so engineers can capture and preserve its glistening character.
fields.practical_application: An engineer uses a stereo pair placed over the instrument to capture the full shimmer and reverberant tail without close-miking artifacts.
common_mistakes: Adding bright reverb that clashes with the natural overtone shimmer
Close-miking one region and missing the full field of ringing strings
Over-compressing and killing the long ringing decay
scenario_contexts: Recording a santoor solo in Persian or Indian classical music
Placing a santoor's shimmer in a film or ambient mix
Choosing reverb that complements rather than masks the natural decay

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Santur" (hammered dulcimer, multiple metal string courses)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (struck-string decay, overtones, and sympathetic reinforcement)

fields.definition: The soft, continuous, blended texture of the sarangi, a bowed short-necked Indian fiddle whose numerous sympathetic strings resonate with the bowed melody strings to surround each note with a haze of sustained overtones.
fields.plain_english: The wash is the soft, cloudy blanket of sound around a sarangi's melody. The sarangi has many extra strings that ring on their own when you bow, filling the space with a smooth glow behind the tune.
fields.purpose_function: Describes the sympathetic-string resonance that gives the sarangi its vocal, enveloping sound, which engineers aim to capture rather than suppress.
fields.practical_application: A technician mics the sarangi to include the sympathetic strings' resonance, avoiding tight close-miking that would thin out the wash.
common_mistakes: Aggressive noise gating that chops off the sustained resonant tail
Close-miking only the melody strings and losing the sympathetic wash
Mistaking the natural sympathetic resonance for added reverb
scenario_contexts: Recording a sarangi accompaniment in Hindustani classical music
Capturing the vocal-like sustain of a sarangi solo
Preserving sympathetic resonance while controlling bow noise

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Sarangi" (bowed fiddle with sympathetic strings)
"Bowed strings and sympathy, from violins to Indian sarangi" (acoustics study of sympathetic-string resonance, HAL/ASA-indexed research)

fields.definition: A smooth, continuous slide in pitch on the sarod, a fretless plucked lute with a polished metal fingerboard that lets the fingernail glide along the string, producing the seamless pitch transitions (meend) central to Hindustani music.
fields.plain_english: A glissando is a smooth slide from one pitch to another. The sarod has no frets and a shiny metal board, so a player can slide a fingernail along the string and let the note glide, with no steps in between.
fields.purpose_function: Names the continuous pitch-slide technique that the sarod's fretless metal fingerboard makes possible and that defines its expressive, vocal phrasing.
fields.practical_application: An engineer captures the glissando with enough high-frequency detail to keep the sliding fingernail-on-metal character, avoiding heavy filtering that would dull it.
common_mistakes: Confusing a glissando (a smooth slide) with discrete stepped notes
Rolling off the highs and losing the fingernail-slide detail
Using pitch correction that fights the continuous slide
scenario_contexts: Recording a sarod alap full of sliding meend phrases
Editing a sarod line without quantizing the pitch slides
Blending a sarod glissando into a fusion arrangement

sources: Grove Dictionary of Music (Grove Music Online), "Sarod" (fretless metal fingerboard, meend/glissando) and "Glissando"
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments (fretless continuous pitch control on plucked strings)
